steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an NLP paper on topic detection and tracking of news, where we fuse time and text into one document embedding. Motivate the task, explain why existing work underuses timestamps, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Why following news stories matters; need for automatic clustering
- The TDT framework and our focus on event detection
- Gap: time is underused compared to text
- Our time-text model and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - following emerging news stories crucial for real-time decisions on political and public safety matters
  - COVID-19: media platforms, government agencies must spot misinformation early and act
  - humans cannot read all articles -> automatic clustering of news into real-world events
  - also useful for scientific papers, microblogs, online reviews, forum messages, social media posts
- TDT
  - topic detection and tracking framework first introduced in earlier work (cite)
  - our focus: event detection; events = real-world news stories; categorize articles into them
  - topic modeling and clustering-based methods; retrospective and online streaming settings
  - retrospective: all documents together; online: one by one as they appear
- Gap
  - most documents have a timestamp (written, spoken, shared)
  - TDT uses it at least for temporal locality of news events
  - beyond that, focus on text representations (cite), not time
  - time model parameter-free / low capacity, unconnected to text
  - misses how time interacts with topic: calendar position, event duration
  - e.g. stock reports daily; earnings releases quarterly, discussed several days; weather stories short period; movie release weeks or months
- Contributions
  - unified neural time-text model fusing temporal and semantic embeddings
  - time-aware neural document embedding; TDT and other NLP tasks
  - two TDT pipelines (retrospective, online), state of the art on benchmark corpus of recent prior work; retrospective model free of TF-IDF features -> easier to adapt to new domains
  - ablation: sinusoidal positional embedding beats learned positional embedding and Date2Vec
  - analysis: better on recurring events that challenge previous TDT systems

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Following emerging news stories is very important for making real-time decisions on important political and public safety matters. During the COVID-19 pandemic, for example, media platforms and government agencies need to identify misinformation as it emerges and take action in time to protect the safety of the public. Humans cannot read all the articles that the news media produce, so automatic clustering of news articles into real-world events is needed to make this work tractable. Computational tools for this task are useful for organizing not just news articles but also scientific papers, microblogs, online reviews, forum messages, and social media posts.

Earlier work first introduced the topic detection and tracking (TDT) framework to address these needs. In this paper we focus on the event detection part of TDT. Here events are defined as real-world news stories, and we want to categorize news articles into these events. Researchers have proposed topic modeling methods and also clustering-based methods for this task, and both in retrospective and in online streaming settings. In the retrospective setting the news documents are processed all together, while in the online setting they are processed one by one as they appear in the stream.

- Gap
  - most documents have a timestamp (written, spoken, shared)
  - TDT uses it at minimum for temporal locality of news events
  - beyond that researchers focus on text representations, not time
  - time model parameter-free or low capacity, unconnected to text
  - misses how time interacts with topic: calendar position, how long the event lasts
  - examples: stock reports daily; earnings releases quarterly, discussed over several days; weather event short period; movie release weeks or months
- Contributions
  - unified neural time-text model, temporal + semantic embeddings
  - time-aware neural document embedding, TDT and other NLP tasks
  - two TDT pipelines (retrospective, online), state of the art on benchmark corpus of recent prior work; retrospective model free of TF-IDF features, easier domain adaptation
  - ablation: sinusoidal positional embedding beats learned positional embedding and Date2Vec
  - error analysis: better on recurring events

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Following emerging news stories is very important for making real-time decisions on important political and public safety matters. During the COVID-19 pandemic, for example, media platforms and government agencies need to identify misinformation as it emerges and take action in time to protect the safety of the public. Humans cannot read all the articles that the news media produce, so automatic clustering of news articles into real-world events is needed to make this work tractable. Computational tools for this task are useful for organizing not just news articles but also scientific papers, microblogs, online reviews, forum messages, and social media posts.

Earlier work first introduced the topic detection and tracking (TDT) framework to address these needs. In this paper we focus on the event detection part of TDT. Here events are defined as real-world news stories, and we want to categorize news articles into these events. Researchers have proposed topic modeling methods and also clustering-based methods for this task, and both in retrospective and in online streaming settings. In the retrospective setting the news documents are processed all together, while in the online setting they are processed one by one as they appear in the stream.

Most real-world documents have a timestamp, which is the time at which they were written, spoken, or shared. TDT modelers use this metadata at least to exploit the temporal locality that is inherent in news events. But beyond that, researchers tend to focus on improving text representations and not time representations. The time model is usually parameter-free or low capacity, and it is not connected to the text. This misses important ways in which the time can interact with the topic of the article and influence where it falls on the calendar and how long it lasts as an event. For example, stock reports happen daily, but corporate earnings releases can happen quarterly and are discussed over several days. Stories about a weather event are likely written over a short time period, while stories about a movie release may be discussed for weeks or months.

In this paper we address these gaps with a unified neural time-text model, which fuses temporal and semantic embeddings to represent news documents. Our contributions are:

- • We propose a time-aware neural document embedding method, which can be applied to topic detection and tracking and to other NLP tasks.

- • We build two TDT pipelines on top of our time-aware model, one for retrospective and one for online event clustering, and they achieve state-of-the-art performance in both settings on the corpus that recent prior work used as a benchmark. Our retrospective model also does not need the TF-IDF features that similar systems need, so it can be adapted to new domains more easily.

- • We do an ablation analysis on our time representation. We find that sinusoidal positional embedding works better than two alternatives, learned positional embedding and Date2Vec, for encoding timestamps for TDT.

- • We analyze the event predictions of our model and of baseline methods and find that our model handles recurring events better, which are a challenge for previous TDT systems.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Following emerging news stories is crucial to making real-time decisions on important political and public safety matters. Amid the COVID-19 pandemic, for instance, media platforms and government agencies need to identify emerging misinformation in time and take action to protect the safety of the public. As humans cannot read all of the articles produced by the news media, automatic clustering of news articles into real-world events is needed to make this work tractable. Computational tools for this task are useful for organizing not only news articles, but also scientific papers, microblogs, online reviews, forum messages, and social media posts.

[1] first introduced the topic detection and tracking (TDT) framework to address these needs. In this paper, we focus on the event detection part of TDT, where events are defined as real-world news stories and the goal is to categorize news articles into these events. Researchers have proposed both topic modeling and clustering-based methods for this task, in both retrospective and online streaming settings. In the retrospective setting, the news documents are processed all together, whereas in the online setting they are processed one by one as they appear in the stream.

Most real-world documents have a timestamp: the time at which they were written, spoken, or shared. TDT modelers use this metadata, at a minimum, to exploit the temporal locality inherent in news events. Beyond that, however, researchers tend to focus on improving text representations [2,3,4,5] rather than time representations. The time model is typically parameter-free or low capacity, and unconnected to the text. This overlooks important ways in which the time may interact with the topic of the article to influence where it falls on the calendar and how long it lasts as an event. For example, stock reports happen daily, but corporate earnings releases may happen quarterly and be discussed over several days. Stories about a weather event are likely to be written over a short time period, while stories about a movie release may be discussed over weeks or months.

In this paper, we address these gaps with a unified neural time-text model that fuses temporal and semantic embeddings to represent news documents. Our contributions are as follows:

- • We propose a time-aware neural document embedding method that can be applied to topic detection and tracking and other NLP tasks.

- • We build two TDT pipelines based on our time-aware model, for retrospective and online event clustering respectively, achieving state-of-the-art performance in both settings on the corpus used as a benchmark by recent prior work. Importantly, our retrospective model does not need the TF-IDF features required by similar systems, so it can be adapted to new domains more easily.

- • We conduct an ablation analysis of our time representation and find that sinusoidal positional embedding outperforms two alternatives, learned positional embedding and Date2Vec, for encoding timestamps for TDT.

- • We analyze the event predictions of our model and of baseline methods, and find that our model better handles recurring events, which pose challenges to previous TDT systems.
